summary: For ages 7–9, teach fair/comparative testing through the child-language three-variable frame — change one thing, measure one thing, keep everything else the same — anchored in concrete apparatus (ramps and cars, paper planes, plants, dissolving). Build the necessity of controlling variables by letting an unfair test (two things changed at once) become genuinely uninterpretable, so pupils feel why isolation matters rather than only being told. Complement design practice with recognition tasks (spot-the-unfair-test, sort factors into change/measure/keep-same) and justification dialogue, and honestly name when a fair test is the right enquiry type versus observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying, or research.
misconceptions: Thinking a 'fair test' means being nice/taking turns (the everyday meaning of 'fair') rather than a controlled comparison where only one variable changes.
Changing more than one variable at a time and still believing the result is trustworthy — not seeing that you then can't attribute the effect to any single cause.
Believing every scientific question needs a fair test — over-applying it to questions better answered by observing over time, pattern-seeking or research (the AKSIS over-default).
Confusing the variable you change with the variable you measure (mixing up the input and the outcome).
Forgetting the 'keep the same' variables entirely — controlling only the obvious ones and leaving hidden variables uncontrolled.

activities.title: Design the ramp race: isolate one variable
steps: Set up two ramps and a toy car. For each ramp choose values for the conditions: surface (smooth/rough), height, and starting push.
Choose what to measure — e.g. how far the car rolls.
First deliberately make ramp B BOTH rougher AND steeper than ramp A, run both, and try to say which change caused the difference in distance.
Notice you cannot attribute the result to one cause; then rebuild so only ONE condition (e.g. the surface) differs and everything else is identical, and run it again.
Run each set-up more than once and check the result is consistent before concluding.
As you configure, fill in a 'change / measure / keep-the-same' tray recording which variable you changed, which you measured, and which you held constant.
activities.insight: A test is fair because only one thing changed, so a difference in the result that shows up again when you repeat the runs can be put down to that single change; when two things change at once the result cannot tell you which cause produced it.

activities.title: Paper-plane fair test: build it and throw it
steps: Question: do paper aeroplanes fly further with bigger wings? Using paper and a tape measure, set up a fair test to answer it.
Before throwing, state what you will change (wing size), what you will measure (how far each plane flies), and what you will keep the same (same paper, same throwing spot, same thrower, same effort).
Make a prediction, then throw both planes a couple of times, holding the one-variable rule as you go.
Record each throw's distance in a simple two-column results table (changed variable | measured distance).
Compare the results against your prediction and say which variable was changed, which measured, and which kept the same.
activities.insight: Setting up and carrying out a real comparative test requires deliberately holding hidden conditions constant; what you DON'T hold the same (different paper, a harder throw for one plane, a different thrower) is what breaks fairness.

activities.title: Spot the unfair test and sort the variables
steps: Look at a contrast pair of set-ups: one where two things changed and one where only one changed. Decide which is fair and explain why.
For a given test, sort its factors into three columns: what is changed, what is measured, what is kept the same.
Match investigation questions to the right enquiry type — fair test, observing over time, pattern-seeking, classifying/grouping, or researching — and say why a fair test is or isn't the best tool.
activities.insight: Recognising fairness and correctly assigning variable roles reinforces the frame; not every question needs a fair test — some are better answered by observing over time, pattern-seeking, or research.

activities.title: Justify your plan with a science partner
steps: Explain your planned test aloud to a partner or in-role scientist.

Answer probing questions: Why keep the ramp height (or throwing spot) the same? What is the one thing you're changing, and what are you measuring? Name two things you're keeping the same and why they matter.
Hunt for hidden uncontrolled variables you may have missed and adjust your plan.
activities.insight: Being able to justify WHY each condition is held constant — not just list them — shows the reasoning behind fairness and surfaces hidden variables.

checkQuestion: We want to find out whether paper aeroplanes fly further with bigger wings. Here's paper and a tape measure. Set up a fair test to answer it — as you get it ready, show me what you'll change, what you'll measure, and what you'll keep the same. Then do a couple of throws. I'll watch.
checkAnswer: The child changes only the wing size, measures how far each plane flies, and keeps everything else the same — same paper, same throwing spot, same thrower, same effort. They set it up and throw while holding the one-variable rule, and can name which variable is changed, which measured, and which kept the same.
